title: A headline is a promise to the right reader, not a stunt for everyone.
dek: Claude Hopkins treats the headline as the first act of salesmanship: a small piece of language that lets the people who could benefit recognize themselves, and lets everyone else keep moving. Its job is not to make noise. Its job is to make the right interest visible.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: A headline earns attention by being legible to a particular person with a particular need. Cleverness can be useful, but it is not a substitute for making the offer and the reader's stake recognizable.

canon.heading: Hopkins: The headline should reveal the interest it is prepared to serve.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 5, "Headlines," in Claude C. Hopkins's Scientific Advertising. Hopkins makes a sharp distinction between attracting a crowd and selecting a prospect: the opening words must help the right reader recognize a relevant benefit before the rest of the argument has any chance to work.
canon.readerIntro: Read first for Hopkins's view of selection: an ad is unlike a salesperson because it can be ignored, and that is useful when its headline identifies the people it can help. Read again for his discipline of comparison: the writer's taste is not enough; different appeals must be tested against real responses.

blocks.label: 01 / Call the person you can actually help
paragraphs: Hopkins begins with a practical asymmetry. A salesperson must spend time with many people who will never be interested; an advertisement can let disinterested people pass by. The headline therefore has a selective task. Like calling a name in a crowd, it should signal the person whose situation and reason for caring match the offer.

That makes a vague or blind headline expensive even when it creates curiosity. It may collect attention from people who cannot use the offer while failing to tell the most promising reader that the page concerns them. In Hopkins's account, reach without relevance is not the same as an audience.

blocks.label: 02 / Reveal the interest before asking for time
paragraphs: The chapter's newspaper comparison is exact. Readers scan headings to find the subjects they care about, not to reward ingenuity. A story that matters deeply can be missed if its label conceals the subject. For Hopkins, the headline or picture must let the desired prospect see the benefit, problem, or category at a glance.

His point is not that every headline must be literal or joyless. It is that the creative choice has a job: make the relevant interest legible. If the reader must decode what is being offered before deciding whether it matters, the ad has already asked for more attention than it has earned.

blocks.label: 03 / Let response correct your private preference
paragraphs: Hopkins spends more time on headlines than on writing the rest of an ad because the right hearing determines whether the sales argument can work at all. His evidence is comparative: the same story, placed under different headings, can produce radically different returns. The useful appeal varies by product and by audience rather than by the writer's own admiration for it.

The operational lesson is to name competing reader interests, then make a fair test. A product may have many real virtues, but the lead should be the one that brings the largest qualified group into the conversation. Secondary appeals can remain in the body or be given their own treatment once response justifies them.

closeReading: What does Hopkins gain by treating the headline as a selection device rather than a universal attention device?
Why can a clever but blind headline produce more attention and still be commercially worse?
Which reader interest does Hopkins say the headline or picture must make visible before the body copy can matter?
What does the comparison of identical ads with different headlines teach about relying on a writer's own taste?
Choose one current offer. What is the most specific audience, moment, or benefit its headline should reveal immediately?

principle.heading: Make the reader's reason for caring obvious before you make the case.
principle.body: A strong headline does not merely announce a campaign. It identifies a valuable situation and gives the qualified reader a reason to enter. The test is not whether everyone notices it; it is whether the right person can tell, quickly and accurately, that the next paragraph is for them.
principle.example: A scheduling product is introducing automated handoffs. "Work smarter with AI" describes neither a reader nor a stake. "For support leads: hand off an urgent ticket without losing the customer's last three decisions" names the buyer, the moment, and the cost of failure. It may attract fewer casual clicks, but it gives a support lead a concrete reason to read the product story.
principle.practice: Take one live page, email, or campaign. Write three headlines, each built around a different real reader interest: a painful moment, a desired outcome, and a category-specific proof. For each, write the exact audience it excludes. Choose one to test only after you can explain why that exclusion improves the quality of the response.

signals.heading: Three signals that product and distribution teams are still competing for a clearer first promise.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI retires Atlas as it shifts browser capabilities into ChatGPT and Codex
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI's ChatGPT release notes say Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 and direct users to move browser data they want to keep. The note frames the change around browser-based agentic capabilities being brought into ChatGPT and Codex.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A transition notice has to identify the affected user, the deadline, and the next action in the first few lines. This one is a useful operational version of Hopkins's rule: the people with Atlas data can immediately tell that the message concerns them and what they should do.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether the replacement browser workflow makes the migration path as concrete for existing Atlas users as the retirement message does.

fieldNotes.title: Home Depot consolidates technology teams around its customer-experience strategy
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Retail Dive reports that Home Depot moved its store, supply-chain, and Pro-product technology teams under its new EVP and CTO in a reorganisation linked to streamlined core offerings, interconnected shopping, and professional customers.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A customer promise only works when the product experience can deliver it across the journey. The reorganisation makes the strategic audience explicit - DIY and Pro customers navigating connected shopping - and puts the teams behind that promise closer together.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether the structure produces clearer, customer-visible changes for Pro and DIY shoppers rather than a broad technology message with no distinct journey improvement.

fieldNotes.title: Airbnb tests an opt-in AI search experience alongside familiar filters
fieldNotes.whatHappened: TechCrunch reports that Airbnb said AI has reduced time from concept to launch on key initiatives and is testing a toggle for a natural-language, visual AI search experience rather than requiring customers to abandon the filters they already know.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The product proposition is clearer when customers can choose the new discovery mode for the job it is meant to do. An opt-in test keeps the promise specific and gives Airbnb a cleaner way to learn whether the new interface earns use rather than merely generating novelty.
fieldNotes.watch: Which customer intent the AI search becomes best at serving, and whether Airbnb reports success in discovery quality, booking completion, repeat use, or all three.

signals.tweetHeading: One fragment on making a distribution promise specific.

tweets.author: Albinder Dhindsa
tweets.title: A design-first brand makes its expanded Blinkit range explicit
tweets.summary: Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa announces that customers can now find a much larger range of DailyObjects bags, tech accessories, desk essentials, and more on Blinkit. It is a concise distribution message: name the brand, the channel, and the newly available product categories so the interested buyer can act without decoding the claim.
tweets.text:
Back in the day, we (Grofers) were doing B2B deliveries for @daily_objects.

More than a decade later, it’s great to see what Pankaj and Saurav have built. A thoughtful, design-first Indian brand with an incredible range of products.

And now, we get to help take that range to Blinkit customers. You can now find a much larger range of DailyObjects bags, tech accessories, desk essentials and more on Blinkit.

output.heading: Write the first line for a real reader in a real moment.
output.body: After reading, choose one offer that currently begins with a broad claim. Replace it with a headline that reveals the audience, the moment, and the benefit. Keep the broader brand language for later; let the first line earn the right reader's next ten seconds.
